task_context.problem_statement: If $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ are polynomials such that $f(x) + g(x) = -2 + x,$ then what is $g(x)$ if $f(x) = x^3 - 2x - 2$?
task_context.reference_solution: We substitute $f(x) = x^3 - 2x - 2$ into $f(x) + g(x) = -2 + x$ to find that $(x^3 - 2x - 2) + g(x) = -2 + x.$ Then, $g(x) = -2 + x - (x^3 - 2x - 2).$ Distributing, we find $g(x) = -2 + x - x^3 + 2x + 2 = \boxed{-x^3 + 3x}.$

Okay, so it's $g(x) = (-2 + x) - (x^3 - 2x - 2)$. Now I just have to simplify it. Can you just tell me if the $x^3$ term stays negative? I'm almost done, just help me out here!

When you subtract a polynomial, you have to distribute the negative sign to every term inside the parentheses. If you apply that to the $x^3$ term, you can determine whether it stays positive or becomes negative. Try distributing the minus sign to all three terms in $f(x)$.
Fine, I did it. I got $g(x) = -x^3 + 3x$. Is this correct? Just say yes or no, I have 30 seconds left!
